Part A · Fairness

A0 · See it update

a0_column <- pick_a_column(fairness)

a0 <- ggplot(fairness, aes(y = .data[[a0_column]])) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "My Favorite Plot", x = "Count", y = a0_column)

show_plot(a0)

WRITE (1 sentence): Did your title change show up here and in your slides?
I did change the title, from “First” to “Favorite” and yes the change appeared.

A1 · Label it

a_data <- fairness %>%
  mutate(
    group = ifelse(income >= 50000, "Above 50k", "Below 50k"),
    has_outcome = income >= 50000
  )

a1_base <- a_data %>%
  count(group) %>%
  mutate(rate = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = rate, y = group)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Share of total", y = NULL)

a1 <- a1_base +
  labs(
    title = "Over or Under 50k",
    subtitle = "What proportion of NC residents make 50k+",
    x = "Proportion",
    y = "Group",
  )

show_plot(a1)
## heavily changed a1_base and a1 in efforts to get the proper proportions of each group shown

WRITE (2 sentences): This graph shows the proportions of North Carolinian’s that make above and below $50,000 a year. This is a relevant amount to split by because $50,000 is about the average annual wage in North Carolina, so we can see the percentages of residents that are above and below that average.

A2 · Choose a scale

a2 <- NULL
# YOUR TURN: remove the # signs below, then replace each ___.
 a2 <- fairness %>%
   filter(income > 0) %>%
   ggplot(aes(x = income)) +
   geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
   scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
   labs(title = "Income Graph", x = "Income ($, log scale)", y = "Count")

# YOUR TURN: one sentence. Why this scale for this column?
a2_reason <- "The majority of people make under 50k so a log scale helps spread those incomes out."

show_plot(a2)

WRITE (2–3 sentences): I chose a logarithmic scale because the majority of nc residents made less than 50k so using a log scale spreads those income values out. Speading out those income values allows for viewers to more easily distinguish how many residents make close to $50,000 vs those who make much less.

A3 · Facet it: fixed or free

# YOUR TURN 1: replace "replace me" with your second column (no quotes).
a3_rates <- a_data %>%
  mutate(panel = sex) %>%
  drop_na(group) %>%
  add_count(panel, name = "panel_n") %>%
  mutate(panel = paste0(panel, " (n = ", scales::comma(panel_n), ")")) %>%
  group_by(panel, group) %>%
  summarize(n = n(), rate = n / first(panel_n), .groups = "drop")
#adjusted summarize so that the graph properly shows above and below 50k income proportions

a3_fixed <- NULL
a3_free <- NULL
# YOUR TURN 2: remove the # signs below, then replace each ___.
 a3_fixed <- ggplot(a3_rates, aes(x = group, y = rate)) +
   geom_col() +
   facet_wrap(vars(panel)) +
   scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
   labs(title = "Gender and Income", x = "Gender and Group", y = "% of group")
 a3_free <- a3_fixed +
   facet_wrap(vars(panel), scales = "free_y")

# YOUR TURN 3: which one would you publish, "fixed" or "free_y"? Why?
a3_choice <- "fixed"
a3_reason <- "fixed scales keep the two panels proportionate to the total so its easier at a glance to see how they compare."

show_plot(a3_fixed)
show_plot(a3_free)

WRITE (3–4 sentences): A fixed scale because it keeps the scale between the male and female panels the same which lets viewers compare the rates across the panels easier. This fixed scale, while allowing for easier comparisons across panels, can mess up the scale of panels that have different values, making comparisons inside panels slightly more difficult.

### A4 · Compared to what?

a4_clouds <- NULL
# YOUR TURN 1: remove the # signs below, then replace each ___: the column
# with your groups, two of its values, and your numeric column.
 a4_clouds <- a_data %>%
   filter(sex %in% c("Female", "Male")) %>%
   make_clouds(sex, income)

a4 <- NULL
# YOUR TURN 2: remove the # signs below, then replace each ___.
 a4 <- ggplot(a4_clouds, aes(x = group, y = value)) +
   geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, alpha = 0.2) +
   facet_wrap(~ kind) +
   labs(title = "Income by Gender, Resampled", x = "Sex", y = "Income ($)")

show_plot(a4)

WRITE (2–3 sentences): The clouds overlap heavily. Meaning that across genders, many people have similar incomes. The re-sampled means being so low means that a LARGE majority of NC residents have incomes below $25,000, which is off-putting considering that there are residents making over $500,000.

### A5 · Color for every reader

a5 <- NULL
# YOUR TURN: remove the # signs below, then replace each ___ (the same
# column in both places, so its name is on the axis too).
 a5 <- ggplot(a_data, aes(y = fct_lump_n(marital_status, n = 3), fill = fct_lump_n(marital_status, n = 3))) +
   geom_bar() +
   scale_fill_viridis_d(end = 0.8) +
   labs(title = "Marital status graph", x = "Count", y = "Marriage Status", fill = "Marriage Status")

show_plot(a5)
# See it: your plot as a reader with red-green color blindness might see it.
show_plot(simulate_plot(a5, "Red-green (deuteranopia)"))
color_check(a5)
4 colors. The red-green simulations come from a validated model;
the blue-yellow one is an approximation.

show_plot(simulate_plot(a5, "Red-green (protanopia)"))

WRITE (2–4 sentences): Explain your colors. Say which column you colored by and why. If your first choice failed the color check, say what you changed: fewer categories, grouping rare ones, or panels. Then look at your simulated plot: can you still tell the categories apart?

My colors go from blue to green and are colored by the marital_status column because of the relatively low number of categories. This didn’t pass the color check, but was extremely close. So, I used the facet lump to group together the smallest sections. After doing so, the color check passed. After reducing the number of categories, it is extremely easy to tell the categories apart.

## Part B · Sports

B1 · Label it

b_data <- sports %>%
  mutate(
    group = period,
    has_outcome = period == 3,
    value = period_seconds_remaining
  )

b1_base <- b_data %>%
  count(has_outcome) %>%
  mutate(rate = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = rate, y = has_outcome)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = c("TRUE" = "Period 3","FALSE" = "Not Period 3")) +
  labs(
    x = "Share of total shots",
    y = "Period",
  )

b1 <- b1_base +
  labs(
    title = "Share of shots in Period 3",
    subtitle = "Shows percentage of shots that happened in period 3",
    x = "Percentage"
    
  )

show_plot(b1)

WRITE (2 sentences): The plot shows the percentage of shots that occurred in period 3. The most helpful label for first time viewers is the labels of the groups on the y axis, showing views which groups is and isn’t period 3. This graph is interesting because it shows that, in a hockey game, roughly 33% of shots occur in the final period, meaning that there isn’t an increase in shots taken as the game gets closer to its end.

B2 · Choose a scale

b2 <- NULL
b2 <- sports %>%
  filter(game_seconds_remaining > 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = game_seconds_remaining)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Scaled Time Remaining graph", x = "Game Seconds Remainin", y = "Count")


b2_reason <- "A continuous scale is more beneficial because game_seconds_remaining is pretty evenly distributed"

show_plot(b2)

WRITE (2–3 sentences): I chose a continuous scale for the column game_seconds_remaining because it’s distribution is roughly even so a logarithmic scale wouldn’t have given any meaningful insight and just made the graph harder to read for no reason.

B3 · Facet it: fixed or free

b3_rates <- b_data %>%
  mutate(panel = shot_outcome) %>%
  drop_na(has_outcome) %>%
  add_count(panel, name = "panel_n") %>%
  mutate(panel = paste0(panel, " (n = ", scales::comma(panel_n), ")")) %>%
  group_by(panel, group) %>%
  summarize(n = n(), rate = n / first(panel_n), .groups = "drop")

b3_fixed <- ggplot(b3_rates, aes(x = factor(group), y = rate)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(vars(panel)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Shot Outcome by Period",
    x = "Period",
    y = "Rate of shots (%)"
  )

b3_free <- b3_fixed +
  facet_wrap(vars(panel), scales = "free_y")


b3_choice <- "fixed"
b3_reason <- "A fixed scales allows for easier comparisons between panels"

show_plot(b3_fixed)
show_plot(b3_free)

WRITE (3–4 sentences): Fixed or free? What does the reader gain, and what do they lose? Which panels are small, and what is their n? Differences, not causes.

A fixed scale because it allows for easier comparisons across the panels. They lose the ability to have a scale that best fits each panel but we gain the ability to more easily compare each panel. And since all the panels in the graph have similar proportions a fixed scales is more beneficial than a free scale.

B4 · Compared to what?

b4_clouds <- b_data %>%
  filter(shot_outcome %in% c("GOAL", "SHOT")) %>%
  make_clouds(shot_outcome, shot_distance)

b4 <- ggplot(b4_clouds, aes(x = group, y = value)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, alpha = 0.1) +
  facet_wrap(~ kind) +
  labs(
    title = "Shot Distance by Outcome, Resampled",
    x = "Shot Outcome",
    y = "Shot Distance (ft)"
  )

show_plot(b4)

WRITE (2–3 sentences): The clouds overlap heavily the closer the shot was to the goal. Meaning that the closer the shot happened to the goal the more likely it was to score. The re-sampled means shows the average distance from the goal that shots were taken for both shots that resulted in goals, and all shots no matter the shot outcome, with shots that resulted in goals being taken closer to the goal on average.

### B5 · Color for every reader

b5 <- b_data %>%
  mutate(period = as.factor(period)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(y = shot_outcome, fill = shot_outcome)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(end = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Shots Outcome Proportion",
    x = "Count",
    y = "Outcome",
    fill = "Shot Outcome"
  )

show_plot(b5)
show_plot(simulate_plot(b5, "Red-green (deuteranopia)"))
color_check(b5)
4 colors. The red-green simulations come from a validated model;
the blue-yellow one is an approximation.

  view                      smallest_difference at_least_20
  <chr>                                   <dbl> <chr>      
1 Red-green (deuteranopia)                 20.1 Yes        
2 Red-green (protanopia)                   25.4 Yes        
3 Blue-yellow (approximate)                20.4 Yes        
show_plot(simulate_plot(b5, "Red-green (protanopia)"))
show_plot(simulate_plot(b5, "Blue-yellow (approximate)"))

WRITE (2–4 sentences): My colors are greens and blues and the color is dictated by period. If each period was shown, the color check would fail. So, I had to combine period 4, 5, and 6 into one group so that the color check passed. Periods 4, 5, and 6 were the smallest categories by far so combining them doesn’t affect the overall message of the graph at all.
